opus-5.5.text:
I think the GPT-3 moment for robotics is when we have a single foundation model, one set of weights, that you can drop onto a robot and have it do a broad range of tasks reasonably well, zero-shot or with just a little prompting, the way GPT-3 could suddenly do translation, summarization, and code without being trained for each one.

Before GPT-3, NLP was a zoo of specialist models: one for sentiment, one for translation, one for question answering. Robotics today still looks a lot like that. You train a policy for picking up a cup, another for opening a drawer, and each is brittle and tied to a specific robot in a specific lab. The moment I'm waiting for is when that collapses into one generalist model that understands what you want, perceives the world, and outputs actions. It should work across tasks, environments, and ideally across different robot bodies, which I call cross-embodiment.

It won't look exactly like the language case, because robotics has a data problem language never had. For GPT-3 we could scrape the internet. There's no internet of robot motor-control data. So we have to build it from three sources. First, internet-scale video and text, which tell the model how the world works and what humans do. Second, simulation, which gives us essentially unlimited data if we can close the sim-to-real gap. Third, real robot data collected through teleoperation, which is expensive but grounds everything in reality. Mixing those three well is the core recipe.

When will we know we're there? When a researcher can type an instruction to a humanoid in a kitchen it has never seen and it just does something sensible. Not perfectly, since GPT-3 wasn't perfect either, but in a way that makes everyone in the field go, "Oh, this is the paradigm now." That would mean the scaling path is clear and it's an engineering problem rather than a mystery. I think we're closer than most people realize.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a generalist foundation model for robotics but does not place the moment on the System 1 side.

r002.rationale: It discusses tasks and robot bodies broadly, but does not explain that one abstract verb such as “open” requires different motions for different objects.

r003.rationale: It describes a model that understands requests and outputs actions across tasks, but does not identify generalizing abstract action verbs into low-level motor control across varied scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and I think about this a lot. For me, the GPT-3 moment for robotics is when we have a single foundation model that you can prompt with a natural language instruction, in a new environment it has never seen, with a robot embodiment it may not have been trained on extensively, and it just does the task zero-shot. No fine-tuning, no task-specific data collection, no reward engineering by a human in the loop.

Think about what GPT-3 actually did for NLP. Before GPT-3, we had a different model for every task. You had a translation model, a summarization model, a sentiment classifier. GPT-3 collapsed all of that into one model where the task is just part of the prompt. Robotics today still looks like pre-GPT-3 NLP. We have a model for grasping, a model for navigation, a model for a specific manipulation benchmark, each trained on its own dataset, and they don't transfer. The GPT-3 moment is when that collapses into one generalist.

The hard part is data. Language models got lucky because the internet is essentially a free, gigantic dataset of human thought. There is no internet of robot actions. Nobody has uploaded trillions of tokens of motor commands. So the question becomes, where does the scale come from? I think the answer is a combination of three things. Real robot teleoperation data, which is high quality but expensive. Human video, because there are billions of hours of people doing things with their hands on YouTube and it's the closest thing we have to an internet of embodiment. And simulation, which is the only source that is truly unbounded, because you can generate as much as your GPUs can render and physically simulate.

And here is where I think the generative models come in. If you can use language models to write the simulation tasks and the reward functions, and use diffusion or video models to generate the visual diversity, you basically bootstrap a data engine that doesn't depend on human labor. That's what projects like Eureka were trying to show. The LLM writes a reward function, trains a policy, looks at the result, and iterates, and it ends up outperforming the human expert on things like dexterous pen spinning.

So the GPT-3 moment is less a single demo and more a phase transition. You will know it has happened when a startup can build a new robot product by writing a prompt instead of hiring a team of roboticists for a year. My bet is humanoids will be the form factor where this shows up first, simply because the world is built for the human body, so the data from human video transfers the most directly, and one body plan can address the largest number of tasks. I don't think it's a decade away. I think it's closer to a few years, and it will feel sudden when it comes, just like GPT-3 did.

r003.rationale: The response hopes for zero-shot task performance across environments and embodiments, but does not identify generalizing abstract action verbs into low-level motor control across varied scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I think a GPT-3 moment for robotics would be when we have a single model that can generalize to tasks it wasn’t explicitly trained to do. You could put a robot in a new environment, give it an instruction, and it would figure out how to accomplish that task without collecting a new dataset and retraining for that specific situation.

The key is that it shouldn’t just work for one robot in one lab. We’d want a model that can transfer across environments, objects, and ideally different robot bodies. You might need a little adaptation, but you wouldn’t be starting from scratch every time.

And it doesn’t have to be perfect. GPT-3 wasn’t perfect either. What made it exciting was that you could start to see this broad capability emerge from a general training approach. For robotics, that would be the moment when we stop building a separate system for every task and start getting new behaviors out of the same foundation model.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, a GPT-3 moment for robotics would be when we have one general-purpose model that can control many different robots and do tasks it wasn’t explicitly trained to do. You could ask it, in natural language, to do something new, and it would draw on what it has learned to figure it out, rather than requiring a separate training pipeline for every task.

The key is generalization. A robot doing one impressive demonstration is exciting, but can the same model work in a different room, with unfamiliar objects, or on a different robot? When we can scale training and see those capabilities transfer reliably, that would feel like a GPT-3 moment.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general-purpose model and transfer, but does not mention or identify the System 1 side.
